en: Auspicious Invocation [K fol. 1r] [Siddham] Homage to the feet of the venerable True Guru!
Śrīnivāsa, whose nature is incomparable bliss, is the non-abode.

Victorious is the lotus-handed one, who possesses the knowledge of the forms of the ten incomparable goddesses, who is endowed with wisdom, who brings about the attainment of welfare and happiness for the three worlds, and who remains changeless as long as the quarters of space expand. (1)

Homage to the Vajra of the Universal Body, Speech, and Mind. "Anupama" (Incomparable), and so forth. The connection is as follows: the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara, who has a lotus (*kamala*)—that is, a *padma*—in his hand, is victorious. Of what nature is he? He is described as such because his form (*rūpa*), which is his very essence (*svabhāva*), is bliss itself that is devoid of comparison; for there exists nothing else endowed with qualities such as being most excellent, greatness, and the state of not abiding in *saṃsāra*, with which it could be compared. Thus he is called "Incomparable."

Furthermore, what are his specific qualities? *Śrī* (Glory) is characterized by the accumulation of merit and wisdom; he whose abode or support is that is thus described. Because he is omnipresent by virtue of having the nature of the *dharmakāya*, and because there is no fixed dwelling for him, he is "without abode" (*anivāsa*).

Again, of what kind is he? He is "with the sciences" (*savidya*), meaning he has as his attendants the ten goddesses, from Rūpavajrā to Tārā, who are "incomparable" (*nirupamā*) because they transcend all comparison due to their possession of supreme beauty, youth, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and so forth. He exists together with the science that is his own essential nature (*svābhā-rūpa-vidyā*), and is therefore "with the science" (*savidya*).

The welfare of the three worlds—that is, of the people dwelling within the three worlds—is that which is beneficial for the future, such as Buddhahood and the like; happiness is that which is beneficial for the present, such as the state of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and the like. The attainment of this [welfare and happiness] is its realization; he whose nature is the "making" (*kāra*) of that is thus described. Because he possesses the quality of not passing into final nirvana and because his form is non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), there is an absence of transformation characterized by change; therefore, he is "unchanging" (*avikāra*). Thus distinguished, the Blessed One is victorious.

He states for how long [this lasts]: "As long as there is the expansion of hope" (*yāvad āśāvikāśāḥ*). "Hope" (*āśā*) refers to the ten directions whose nature is space; or else, "hope" refers to the thirst for existence and enjoyment belonging to all sentient beings. Their "expansions" (*vikāśāḥ*) mean their opportunities, their occurrences, that is to say, their manifestations. As long as these exist, so long does the Blessed One triumph; the meaning is that he remains superior to all others, such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha.

Here, by the phrase "one whose form is incomparable bliss," the fulfillment of one's own welfare (*svārthasaṃpatti*) is stated. By the phrase "abode of glory" (*śrīnivāsa*), the means for that [fulfillment] is indicated, because the two accumulations of merit and gnosis are expressed by the term "glory" (*śrī*). By the phrase "cause for the attainment of the welfare and happiness of the three worlds," the fulfillment of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpatti*) is stated.

By the phrase "possessing the vidyā of the form of the ten peerless goddesses" (*savidyas*), the means for that [fulfillment of others' welfare] is indicated; for it is impossible to effect the fulfillment of the welfare of others in all its aspects through a body devoid of the forms of the ten goddesses, the thirty-two major marks, and the eighty minor marks.
[End of section on] Purpose and so forth.
Those who do not clearly understand the form of the fourth consecration— which is contained within the illustrious mantra-discipline and is devoid of explicit words—
[cannot grasp it] through the sevenfold divisions crowded with various multitudes of instructions.
An effort is made for their clear understanding. (2)

By the term *śrīmantranīti*, which denotes general Yoga Tantras, the *Śrīsamāja* is also intended, because the fourth meaning [of the word "glorious"] is not possible elsewhere. The rest is easily understood. It is "crowded with the multitude of instructions from various masters" and "confused by the seven divisions," which comprise the mass of instructions received by masters of the past, future, and present. It is for the sake of "clear comprehension" (*sphuṭāvagati*), that is, for the sake of easy and clear realization.
All non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) possess confused understanding regarding both reality (*tattva*) and the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Regarding the knowledge of the nature of reality and that which is to be accomplished, it is indeed a popular saying among people that the Vedāntin is the one who knows reality most excellently compared to them. (3)

"Confused," and so forth. Those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) whose cognition—that is, their specific form of wisdom—is confused or bewildered, are described as such. All non-Buddhists indeed have the eye of their intellect impaired by the cataract of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. They are deluded regarding the cognition—the realization—of the true nature of reality and the nature of that which is to be established, thinking "this is reality" and "this is the goal to be proven. The remainder is easily understood.

If it is asked: "Since reality (*tattva*) and the goal (*sādhya*) are of a single nature insofar as both are to be adopted (*upādeya*), why are they designated separately as 'reality' and 'the goal'?"—this is incorrect. For although reality is to be adopted, it pervades the entire mass of appearances, such as pleasure, pain, and equanimity. The goal, however, while also being to be adopted, is characterized by desire (*icchā*) consisting in the avoidance of what is undesired; furthermore, although it is to be adopted, it is necessarily intended by all living beings as something to be accomplished through the exclusion of what is not to be accomplished. Thus, there is no fault. [The following are] the goals of the Vedāntins, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas.
In that regard, he first states the probandum (sādhya) as accepted by the Vedāntin: "of the nature of bliss," and so forth.
The Vedāntins maintain that the probandum is of the nature of bliss, self-known, unshakable, and peaceful.
The Śrāvakas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and the Victors, desire the cessation of the substrate consisting of form and the other aggregates.

"Of the nature of bliss" means because it is always composed of happiness. "Self-known" means because, being of the nature of light, it shines by itself. "Unshakable" means because, due to its permanence, it cannot be moved. "Peaceful" means because it is conceived as being devoid of the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*). They "dwell upon" such an object of attainment; that is, they desire it.

Those Pratyekabuddhas who exist together with Śrāvakas—those "rhinoceros-like" Victors (*khaḍgajina*) who are like the horn of a rhinoceros, both those who wander alone and those who move in groups—they desire a goal. What kind of goal? Cessation from the substrata of form and so forth; that is to say, the cessation, the cutting off, the extinction of the substrata characterized as the aggregates (*skandha*) of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. [E~DH~ p.]

This is what is meant: although there is a distinction between *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have undertaken to realize as their goal only *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Now, regarding the fourfold goal favored by the proponents of the Pāramitā system, he says "empty of aspects" (*ākāraśūnya*), and so forth.
Empty of mental constructs, having the form of the moon in the sky, to be personally realized, and possessing the essence of compassion;
adorned with the excellent marks, it brings about the welfare of others.
The outflow of generosity and so forth is devoid of happiness. || 5 ||

They declare that the goal to be accomplished is one whose limbs are adorned with the marks of blissful existence, who is enjoyed by those established on the ten stages, and who acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
They abide in the method of the six perfections, beginning with generosity. || 6 ||

In the Pāramitānaya, that which is first to be accomplished is empty of various forms such as blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, and so forth, and is thus formless (*nirākāra*). For this very reason, its nature (*rūpa*) or essence is such that it is like the sky in being formless, yet like the moon in its luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). It is "to be personally realized" (*pratyātmavedya*), meaning it is to be known solely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) is the desire to uplift the entire world from suffering or the causes of suffering; that itself is the "flavor" (*rasa*) or essence, and thus it is described as such.

This is what is meant: that which is empty of variegated forms such as blue and yellow, free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*), stainless (*nirañjana*), comparable to the sky, lucid, effecting the welfare of the entire world, endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), to be personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedya*), and designated by the terms of the teachings on the perfections (*pāramitā*)—this is the first goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the *Pāramitānaya*.
The second goal to be accomplished in the *Pāramitānaya* is as follows:

These are the beautiful marks known as the thirty-two major characteristics (*dvātriṃśallakṣaṇa*); it is adorned by them. Its nature or essence is to act for the benefit of people—that is, to accomplish their purpose; thus it is "beneficial. It is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), such as generosity, being a result concordant with its cause due to arising from their excellence. Because suffering has already been abandoned previously, and because even pleasure is absent at the stage of direct realization, it is "devoid of pleasure" (*apagatasaukhya*) in the sense that it consists of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This is what is meant: the second object of accomplishment is one's own self in the form of a Perfectly Awakened Buddha—possessing a body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, acting for the benefit of the entire world through the power of practicing the perfections such as generosity, and being of the nature of equanimity by virtue of being free from both pleasure and pain.
In the system of the Perfections (pāramitānaya), this is the third object of accomplishment.

“With joy,” and so forth. That which exists together with joy (*ānanda*) is “with joy” (*sānanda*). This refers to that which possesses limbs adorned with excellent marks, being enjoyed and made subservient by means of the teaching of the Dharma. By whom? By the lords of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*), because it is not within the range of those residing on the remaining stages. In other words, it is being enjoyed by Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, and others who have attained the ten stages.

This is what is meant: in the world-realm of the Perfectly Awakened One known as Ghanavyūha, situated above the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the Blessed One—whose nature is bliss and who consists of the *saṃbhogakāya*—manifests for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the entire world through the gateway of emanation (*nirmāṇa*). His body is invisible even to the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and those who rule over the nine stages; he shines forth until the end of saṃsāra, being experienced solely by the Bodhisattvas who rule over the ten stages through the gateway of hearing the Dharma. It is that very state which is to be accomplished; this is the third [object of attainment]. In the Pāramitā system, there is a fourth object of attainment.
Having completely fulfilled all qualities such as generosity and having performed the entire activity of a Perfectly Awakened One,
that which is the direct realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is [the state of Buddhahood].
That too exists as something to be accomplished, having the nature of cessation. || 7 ||

"Having fulfilled," and so forth. The perfections (*pāramitās*) such as generosity (*dāna*) are themselves the "qualities" (*guṇas*), in the sense that they are "repeatedly practiced" (*guṇyante*). Having fulfilled them—that is, having made them complete—and having also performed all the duties of the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddhas*), which are entirely necessary to be done, there remains a further goal to be accomplished: the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and consists in the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta-nirodha*). Those who abide in the system of the Perfections (*pāramitānaya*) speak thus, asserting that this is the fourth goal to be accomplished. In the Mantra system (*mantranaya*), the goal to be accomplished is sevenfold. In the Mantra system, the first goal to be accomplished is as follows: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with the phrase "the first goal to be accomplished. The following section would typically detail the specific stages of the *kriyā*, *caryā*, *yoga*, and *anuttarayoga* tantras.*
Now, in order to explain the sevenfold object of accomplishment taught in the Mantra system, he says: "Embraced by one's own natural consort," and so forth.
[The object] brings benefit to beings, is embraced by one's own natural consort, and has liberation as its very form, being free from both suffering and pleasure.
They declare that the one to be accomplished is adorned with the eighty secondary marks, free from conceptual construction, and perfect.

That which has the nature (*śīla*) or disposition (*svabhāva*) to embrace its own natural consort (*svābhāṅganā*) is "embracing its own natural consort" (*svābhāṅganāśleṣi*). "Free from conceptualization" (*apetakalpa*) means devoid of conceptual construction (*vyapagatakalpa*), that is to say, free from mental fabrication (*kalpanā*). The rest is easily understood. This is the meaning: first, the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) is the form of equanimity (*upekṣārūpa*), whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and which embraces its own natural consort while acting for the benefit of the world. In the Mantra system, the second object of accomplishment is devoid of the specific form of one's own deity.
Having already clearly conceived of that bliss which is manifest,
called "Great Bliss" (mahāsukha), which effects the welfare of the world and resembles a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), someone said: (9)

"By the form of one's own deity," and so forth. It is empty of the specific form of one's own chosen deity—that is to say, it is formless. Having first of all, immediately after the initial instruction, conceived of bliss independent of the deity’s form, and having realized it through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it becomes clearly manifest and is designated as "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*). And that [bliss], which effects the welfare of the world, is equal in nature to the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).

This is what is meant: immediately following the instruction, that which is devoid of the forms of mantra, mudrā, and deity, made manifest through meditative cultivation, designated as "great bliss," a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), acting for the benefit of the world, resembling an illusion (*māyopama*), and persisting until the end of *saṃsāra*—this is the second object of attainment. Having established the third object of attainment in the Mantra system, one directly [attains] one's own lord (*svādhipa*) in the form of bliss.
Subsequently, having abandoned even mere bliss, the fruit would be attained;
for it is impossible to effect the pure [state] directly, therefore the form of one's own lord has been meditated upon. (10)

"Having performed," and so forth. Having made one's own lord—that is, one's chosen deity—manifest before one, [visualizing him] as having a blissful form, whose sole intrinsic nature is happiness; and subsequently, having abandoned the form of the deity, the result to be accomplished would be established as mere happiness.

Now, if even after having directly realized it the form of the deity must be abandoned, then why was it not manifested at the very beginning? Why was mere bliss alone—not manifested like the second object to be accomplished—not manifested instead? Why this futile exertion? To this he says: "Pure," and so forth. Pure—that is, absolute bliss devoid of the form of the deity—cannot be directly realized at all, because bliss devoid of form is never perceived.

Therefore, for that reason, the third [stage] is that the form (*ākāra*) has been cultivated by one’s own lord. This is the meaning: having meditated upon bliss as being indeed permeated by the form of the deity, and once the form of the deity has become manifest, one leaves it aside; the goal to be accomplished is bliss alone, endowed with the aforementioned qualities.
In the Mantra system, the fourth goal to be accomplished is a body equal to space, its limbs adorned with the [major and minor] marks.

Another proclaims the goal to be filled with incomparable bliss, united with its own nature, manifesting along with immeasurable lords of sages, effecting the welfare of all sentient beings, and yet empty of annihilation. (11)

"Like the sky," and so forth. His body is like the sky, resembling an illusion, and incapable of withstanding analysis. His limbs are adorned with the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). He is filled with incomparable pleasures—so called because they transcend all comparison due to the absence of any analogue for their qualities such as grossness, continuity, flowing until the end of *saṃsāra*, and being free from outflows (*anāsrava*)—extending to the very tips of his pores. And he is united with, that is, embraced by, his own consort who is likewise of such a nature.

By means of the lords of sages, who are thus manifested as infinite and quivering emanations, he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings. "By annihilation" means by cessation; it is empty, trivial, and void.

This is what is meant: it is like the sky, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, the moon in water, a reflection, and a dream; devoid of the nature of being one or many, of existence or non-existence, and of subject or object; without beginning or end; having the nature of the entire collection of all things; without appearance, stainless, transcending all comparisons; having the nature of the *dharmakāya* by virtue of being the form of wisdom that is supremely subtle and profoundly deep; with a body adorned with the thirty-two marks and limbs resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics.

Endowed with supreme passion, youth, and so forth, his limbs embraced by his own consort, he—through the gateway of enjoying the supreme bliss whose nature is the signless pleasure of infinite varieties, together with the host of goddesses beginning with Rūpavajrā and ending with Tārā, like a reflection—[E~DH~ p.]

Being experienced through its noble form imbued with compassion, it is the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*; for the sake of maturing disciples with diverse inclinations, it consists of the *nirmāṇakāya* by virtue of its activity of emanating and reabsorbing infinite Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within various families through manifold kinds of miracles; and it is the nature of non-abiding nirvāṇa, a dharma that remains as long as saṃsāra exists, filled with sublime bliss produced from the samādhi of pure wisdom and skillful means, whose essence is the bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion.
The fourth goal to be accomplished is the emptiness of cessation, by virtue of its being a continuous stream like the flame of a stainless, windless, and motionless lamp.
In the Mantra system, having established the fifth goal as one's own lord (*svādhipa*) manifest in a blissful form, [one proceeds].
Having abandoned [all else], there would be as its fruit merely the knowledge of equanimity—
abiding throughout the cycle of existence, accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings,
resembling a wish-fulfilling gem, and characterized by absolute peace. || 12 ||

"Having performed," and so forth. Having directly manifested one's own lord (*svādhipa*), and subsequently having abandoned it, that which is the knowledge consisting of equanimity (*upekṣā*)—that alone would be the fifth goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The rest is easy to understand. This is what is meant: having directly manifested the form of the maṇḍala circle, and subsequently having dissolved it, the fifth goal to be accomplished would be the mere knowledge of equanimity. In the Mantra system (*mantranaya*), having established the sixth goal, the maṇḍala is directly [manifested] as a blissful form.
Subsequently, there is his own cessation according to his will;
for in this state, there is neither the absence of the welfare of sentient beings nor its manifestation, since [the Buddha] has passed into cessation.
"Having performed," and so forth. Having directly constructed the maṇḍala together with the sāta, its *nirvṛti*—that is, its cessation—is according to one's own will.

Now, one might object: "If, even after having directly realized [the truth], one were later to suppress it at will, then there would be an absence of compassion that has been cultivated over a long period of time. And because of its absence, there would be an absence of the welfare of sentient beings. Anticipating this concern, he says: "Is there also an absence of the welfare of sentient beings, or not? and so forth. In this position, there is no absence of the welfare of sentient beings, because from the wheel that has entered *nirvṛti*—provided it is permeated by compassion—the manifestation of the welfare of sentient beings occurs.

By this he says the following: having directly realized this very wheel in its entirety and having maintained it for as long as desired, one should subsequently remain after bringing about its cessation in every respect, like a lamp. When, however, there arises a desire for the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*), then the welfare of sentient beings should be accomplished by generating another wheel from that very [wheel] which has ceased.

Even upon the generation of another wheel, the attainment of what is desired by those to be trained (*vineya*) occurs according to their respective capacities from that wheel which has long since ceased; thus is the sixth [point].
In the Mantra system, the seventh *sādhya* is as follows:
Having clearly manifested their desired form, someone later declares cessation to be the fruit;
for cessation is of an undifferentiated nature.
Therefore, even though there is a difference in the positions [of the disputants], there is no difference [in the nature of the object]. || 14 ||

"Having performed," and so forth. Since one of the six alternatives is to be established as the result, whatever is desired should first be directly realized; subsequently, like a lamp, it must be completely extinguished, and thereafter one must directly realize that which is devoid of the welfare of sentient beings and so forth.

One might object: "Since there are six distinct positions (*pakṣa*), would there not be six types of cessation (*nirodha*)? How then can it be said that there is only one cessation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of undivided nature," and so forth. That which has an undivided form is "of undivided nature. For although there is a distinction among cessations characterized by the six positions, there is no actual difference [between them], because cessation is identical in its singular nature as non-existence (*abhāva*). This is the meaning: having directly realized any one of the positions, the subsequent cessation—which consists in the cutting off of the continuum of that [position]—is the seventh thing to be established (*sādhya*). [End of Section on Disputes regarding the Fourth Consecration] The first dispute regarding the fourth consecration.
Beyond the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) is the tasting of the bodhicitta; that fourth consecration is the supreme,
because all effort in meditations [is for its sake].
It is useless, because its result is already established. || 15 ||

"Prajñājñāna," and so forth. Some say that the fourth consecration (*caturtha-seka*) is the tasting with the tongue of the *bodhicitta* in the form of nectar, which occurs after the instruction on the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*). However, that is inferior (*avara*), meaning base or lowly. Why is it inferior? Because all the effort—characterized by repeated practice in the meditations on the forms of mantras, mudrās, deities, and so forth—spoken by the Tathāgata, would have been rendered useless.

Why? Because that fruit—the fruit to be accomplished through cultivation—is already established and attained at the very moment of tasting the *bodhicitta*; that is to say, because there is no other distinct fruit [to be obtained].
This concludes the second misconception regarding the fourth consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which follows the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) and concerns the attainment of the consort (*rāmā*).
The taste [of the fourth] is called the lowest consecration;
because all effort directed toward meditation and so forth, as taught by the Buddha, would be fruitless and futile [therein]. (16)

"Wisdom," and so forth. The "fourth consecration" (*turya-seka*) is the savor obtained through the meditative union (*samāpatti*) with those women (*rāmā*) who were acquired after the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), according to how they were encountered. That too is inferior. The remainder has its meaning already explained.
This is the commentary on the scripture.

Now, the fourth [empowerment] is explained as "that again likewise" (*tat punas tathā*). "The fourth" refers to the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), which is called the fourth in relation to the third. "That" (*tat*)—by this word, that very same wisdom-knowledge is referred to in its specific form. "Again" (*punas*)—by the word "again," a distinction from that [previous state] is indicated. And here, the distinction is characterized by being untainted (*anāsrava*), unsurpassed (*niruttara*), utterly expanded, and flowing in an uninterrupted continuity. "Likewise" (*tathā*)—by the word "likewise," suchness (*tādṛśatva*) is expressed.

The meaning of the word *tathā* (thus) is that by whatever kind of causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—endowed with wisdom and so forth—a particular wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) has arisen, it arises subsequently in exactly that same way and through that very same causal complex, and not otherwise.

And here, the meaning should be understood through the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). That by which something is characterized is the "characteristic"—namely, the directly experienced wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)—because that which is not being perceived cannot function as a characteristic, according to the logical principle that "there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) having been apprehended. That which is characterized, known, or explained is the "characterized," namely, the fourth [empowerment] which is about to be directly realized.
Regarding the fourth empowerment, there is a misconception concerning the third.

Regarding this, some maintain that there is no fourth [alternative]. But surely there exists that term "the fourth. How then can it be said that it does not exist? True; however, for the sake of preserving the instruction and to avoid confusing sentient beings, the Blessed One spoke of the third itself using the word "fourth. Otherwise, he would not have said, "that again. That [objection] is utterly inconsistent, because the fourth has been established as proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and will be further demonstrated. This concludes the investigation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*).

In this context, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*)—which is wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)—is indeed recognized by all. However, there is confusion regarding the object of definition (*lakṣya*). That is now investigated. For the object of definition must be either of the nature of an object (*artha*) or of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). It cannot first be of the nature of an object, because the object itself does not exist, as it has been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through its lack of being either one or many. Furthermore, since in the Mantra system (*mantranaya*) the Vijñānavāda and Madhyamaka views are primarily predominant, [the object] must be of the nature of knowledge. And knowledge is either with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*).
There are the following conceptual alternatives: it may be with form, either as a single variegated non-dual form or as multiple forms.

-3.25ex -1ex -.2ex 1.5ex .2ex The Refutation of Cognitions with Aspects (*sākāra-vijñāna*) Regarding this, the proponents of aspectless cognition (*nirākāra-vādin*) declare that cognition with aspects does not exist in any way whatsoever, like a lotus in the sky. [Objection: But surely aspects appear through direct perception in the form of blue, yellow, white, and so forth, as well as jars, cloths, carts, and the like. Since these do not exist as external objects, they must be of the very nature of cognition. Therefore, how can it be said that cognition with aspects does not exist? [Response: It is true that aspects indeed appear; however, they do so in a false (*alīka*) form.

Furthermore, falsity (*alīkatva*) is established by the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely as being devoid of both unity and multiplicity. Since that nature of valid cognition has been explained elsewhere, it is not elaborated upon here. And when falsity is established, forms that are like illusions appear as having the nature of error. Upon the cessation of error, the ultimate reality is proven to be indeed formless, resembling pure crystal.
Therefore, the two conceptual alternatives—that consciousness exists as a manifold non-dual form or as a multiform with aspects—are refuted.

–3.25ex –1ex –.2ex 1.5ex .2ex An Argument for Formless Cognition: Now, it may be objected that even formless cognition, though meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived even in a dream. How, then, can it be said to exist in an ultimate sense? It is replied: cognition in the form of pleasure (*sukha*), whose nature flashes forth within, is indeed experienced as being formless. However, forms such as blue and so forth appear as false.

Otherwise, if those [aspects] were real, all aspects would have to be real. For in that case, even the state of subject and object (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) and so forth would be real. Consequently, since everything would appear as real, there would follow the undesirable consequence of universal liberation, because no false appearance in the form of an illusion would ever appear to anyone. As it has been said: "Reality must be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated."

Therefore, even if one does not wish it, the falsity of the forms such as blue must be accepted. Pleasure and so forth are perceived as being true and formless; how then could they not be perceived? [Objection: But surely consciousness is perceived as having a form, namely the form of pleasure and so forth, because pleasure and the like have the nature of being forms. Furthermore, a cognition devoid of the form of pleasure and so forth is not experienced even in a dream. Since all delusions have vanished on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), it is there that [cognition] attains the characteristic of being perceptible; regarding this point as well, there is no means of proof other than an oath.

That is incorrect, because it fails to understand our intention. We maintain that consciousness—possessing the very form of pleasure and so forth, yet devoid of forms such as blue—is indeed formless (*nirākāra*). Since this is established by the means of valid cognition of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pramāṇa*) and exists for all living beings even at this very moment, how can it not be perceived?

[Objection: But even that [consciousness] is merely false and nothing but an illusion, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many; for the state of being devoid of a nature that is either one or many pervades both consciousness with form (*sākāra*) and consciousness without form (*nirākāra*).

Now, by this reasoning, since all cognition—whether with or without aspects—is established as unreal, there would be no ultimate reality whatsoever. How, then, could the nature of the object of characterization be apprehended through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? This is not a fault; for even though unreality is established through valid cognition in the Madhyamaka system, the form of the subject (*dharmin*), which is a mere appearance like an illusion and devoid of a nature of being either one or many, is not negated.

And precisely within that which is false—a mere appearance—the unimpeded establishment of the definitions and the defined, of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, of the maṇḍala wheels and so forth, as well as the purposeful activity for the entire world, is proven. Thus it has been said:
"One should establish Buddhahood and the state of Vajrasattva by means of the conventional alone."

[Objection: Surely the entire collection of entities is essence-less because it has a false nature; therefore, for what purpose is the exertion of meditating on the maṇḍala-circle and so forth performed? [Response: This is incorrect, because of the statement: "Effort is made even though there is no liberator, for the sake of abandoning false superimposition. Although, when investigated, there is no ultimately real nature of an entity, nevertheless, the craving—"May I be happy, may I not be miserable"—exists in all living beings.

Just as, despite being equally false, one experiences joy from seeing a pleasant dream and dejection from seeing an unpleasant dream, and consequently engages in the recitation of the true Dharma, the chanting of mantras, and so forth, in order to dispel them; likewise, although there is no difference in their falsity, those who possess discernment and seek [enlightenment] will engage in [the path] for the sake of abandoning ordinary conceptualizations such as suffering and for the attainment of the characteristic of perfect awakening. This concludes the investigation into the essential and the non-essential among the seven types of objects to be accomplished.

But surely, that very purpose for which this undertaking was begun has come to naught; for it was the investigation of the *lakṣya* (the object to be defined) and the *lakṣaṇa* (the definition) that was introduced here, and that has been forgotten—it is not known where it has gone.
But was it not indeed accomplished through the sevenfold division?
True, but only according to the maxim of the "molasses and milk" (*guḍa-gorasa-nyāya*). For it is not known whether that [result] is essential or non-essential.
It is said:

The worthlessness of the first [position] is due to the absence of the sequence prescribed by the Mantra-naya (*mantranaya*), the futility of the cultivation of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-bhāvanā*), and the lack of logical justification. For that which possesses the complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*) necessarily comes to be; otherwise, it would not possess the complete causal complex at all. At the stage of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa-avasthā*), that [result] exists with its complete causal complex; therefore, it must necessarily come to be through that. And if it were to exist [only then], there would be a loss of the first [position].

The second [alternative] lacks essence. Since nothing is perceived that is devoid of the form of a body and so forth and consists solely of pleasure, the second has no reality. For that which is ascertained by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is what should be cultivated by a discerning person, not just anything at random. It is only that which is conjoined with a form established by valid cognition that is always perceived; it alone appears as desirable to all people.

Therefore, because there is no interest in the solitary [pleasure], because that which is conjoined with the form of a wheel is never perceived, and because it is impossible to realize [it directly], the second is a mere conceptual construction.

The third [position] lacks substantiality because it is impossible to abandon that which has become one's own nature (*sātmībhūta*)—since its essence is the true object free from afflictions—and because there is no distinction in its integrated form, as well as a lack of purpose; thus, the third possesses no excellence. For instance, when identity is established through simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), the abandonment of one necessarily entails the abandonment of the other, or else neither is abandoned at all.
[Now follows] the investigation into the substantiality and lack of substantiality of the fourth [position].

Because it involves much effort due to its conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and because it is incapable of withstanding analysis, being of the nature of error and lacking the nature of ultimate reality, the third alternative is not auspicious. On this point, some offer the following reasoning: even in the absence of conceptual proliferation, as long as there is the exertion required for the repeated cultivation and eventual direct realization of subtle objects such as the *bindu*, such effort is possible in every case involving an object of meditation. Therefore, if one fears such effort, then nothing at all should be cultivated.

If it is argued that this is because [the former] has the nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then what is the difference between proliferation and non-proliferation during the state of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? Is it not the case that non-proliferation becomes stable much more quickly? This is indeed the distinction. There is both scripture and reasoning for the fact that the mind becomes stable precisely upon that object toward which it is repeatedly directed, continuously and for a long period of time. Thus it has been said:

"Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely cultivated, when the power of cultivation is perfected, that results in a clear and non-conceptual cognition."* *Source: Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā, verse 3599.*
And it is said again:
"Alas, what indolence! Alas, what delusion!
Alas, how crooked this person is toward the true goal!"
Buddhahood, which is bound to nothing other than one's own mind and is not far away, is nevertheless not cultivated.
Thus, this distinction does not hold.

Since the lack of ultimate reality due to having the nature of error is possible in every object that is a subject of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nothing at all would be fit for cultivation. Consequently, cultivation on the entire path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*) would be rendered useless. If it is argued that even that which has the nature of error becomes faultless when cultivated by way of entering into the form of being like an illusion (*māyopama*), [we reply: surely this entry into the form of an illusion is the same even in the case of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Even in that case, what room is there for fault? Therefore, whether it be with elaboration (*prapañca*) or without elaboration (*aprapañca*), whatever is pleasing—whether it accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or otherwise—that very thing should be meditated upon by those seeking Mahāmudrā, setting aside indolence. Enough of this excessive digression.
Furthermore, the distinction between what is essential and what is not here must be understood only by those who have served their gurus.
This concludes the lack of essence regarding the fifth [point].

The fifth [position] is not free from defects, because it suffers from the faults stated regarding the third position, due to its lack of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*), the absence of purpose, and the absence of the sequence of the Mantra system (*mantranaya*).

[Objection: But surely there is the application of the Mantra system prior to direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). So how can there be an absence of it? [Reply: True; however, the state of the direct fruit (*sākṣātphalāvasthā*) is what is to be accomplished. And in that [state], that sequence does not exist directly. Furthermore, we see no purpose in its abandonment. Thus, the sixth [position] is insubstantial.

Because it is impossible to bring about cessation by one's own will, because there is no purpose [in doing so], and because there is no longer any welfare for sentient beings, the conceptualization of the fivefold division of the end is free from blemish. For indeed, the cessation of something occurs either through the cessation of its cause or through the cessation of its pervader (*vyāpaka*). However, in this case, neither a cause nor a pervader that could effect the cessation of one who has directly realized the maṇḍala-circle is observed at the time of [one's] will.

[Objection: But surely emptiness itself is that which brings about cessation. Just as a fire ignited by a mass of wood, having reduced the fuel to ashes without remainder, subsequently ceases of its own accord, so too the fire of the knowledge of emptiness ignited by the maṇḍala-circle will cause even the directly realized maṇḍala-circle to cease. [Response: That is incorrect, because the example is dissimilar. For in that case, the fuel is the cause of the fire.

When the cause, characterized as fuel, ceases, it is indeed logical that the effect, characterized as fire, ceases. But in this case, emptiness is not the cause of the maṇḍala-circle; so for what reason would there be its cessation upon its [emptiness's] cessation? Furthermore, there is no cessation of emptiness.

[Objection: "Granted, let that not be the cause. But emptiness (*śūnyatā*) will be the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Just as when the pervader, 'tree,' is absent, there is the absence of the pervaded, 'śiṃśapā-ness,' so too there will be its [emptiness's] cessation. [Response: This too is without substance. For emptiness, being the nature of reality (*tattva-rūpa*), always pervades the entire circle of all objects of knowledge (*sarva-jñeya-maṇḍala*). And there is never any cessation of it. If there were such a thing, then from the direct realization of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)... [text continues]

Cessation would have to occur either previously or immediately [after realization]. But it does not so happen, because he himself has accepted that even after becoming a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksaṃbuddha), one remains for a certain period of time.

However, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is of the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), and the wheel (*cakra*) is also of the nature of gnosis. Since the gnosis of the wheel does not cease when the gnosis of emptiness arises, by what could the gnosis of emptiness be turned back? Its cessation [by that] does not exist, because there is no opposing factor and because there is an absence of both a cause and a pervader. Therefore, there is no cessation of the gnosis of emptiness, nor is there a cessation of the mandala-wheel from emptiness; thus, emptiness is not something that causes cessation.

Who says that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the cause of cessation? Furthermore, the claim that "whatever causes cessation must be known through the instruction of a guru" is also devoid of substance. Even according to the instruction of a guru, to say that there exists some means of cessation other than emptiness that is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely trivial. Moreover, cessation at every moment consists in the nature of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and pervades all things; it does not cause the cessation of the continuum (*saṃtāna*). Therefore, cessation does not occur by one's own will. Nor do discerning persons have any need for a cessation that is essentially flavorless. As it has been said:
When sentient beings are being liberated, there arise those oceans of joy; surely that alone is sufficient—what need is there for a liberation devoid of flavor?

Thus, there is no benefit for sentient beings even in [the state of] cessation (*nivṛtti*). For no causal efficacy whatsoever is possible in space or in a sky-lotus. The claim that the benefit of sentient beings will arise from a wheel that has long since ceased, being past and lacking the nature of a real entity, is also insubstantial; for it would entail the absurd consequence that even a peacock that died long ago would still produce a sound from its throat. If it is argued that causal efficacies do indeed arise even from space because it serves as a suitable basis (*yogyadhiṣṭhāna*), we reply: they do not. Causal efficacy arises from the mental form itself precisely because it serves as the suitable basis, not from space, because the latter lacks any form (*nīrūpatva*).

[Objection: "But surely, having ceased, the maṇḍala-circle arises again at the time of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*). From that, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) occurs; then it ceases once more, and arises yet again. [Response: This is incorrect. Just as there is no manifestation of the activity for the benefit of sentient beings in reality (*tattvataḥ*), so too it is for the circle. Therefore, the occurrence of purposeful activity is impossible. Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in its arising again after having ceased; enough of this excessive proliferation. Thus ends the seventh [chapter], which concerns its lack of essence.

Since the mass of faults stated regarding the sixth position also exists in the seventh, we do not engage in the "grinding of what is already ground. Now, one might ask: since the seventh is identical to the sixth, how can there be a distinction for the seventh from that? There is indeed a distinction. In the previous state, there was a fixed circular form; here, however, there is cessation at will and production at will. In the seventh, this is not the case. Therefore, they are not identical. And thus it is taught as distinct. [The nature of the fourth consecration: Purified by being washed with the flow from the seed-syllable of the thunderbolt...

The fourth stage, which is the ripening of the grain of the Fourth [Turya], reaches its full maturity— though hidden even from the learned— as the nourishment for the sprout that has become a lotus. 17.
"Thunderbolt," and so forth. This is to be understood through the instruction of a true guru.
The other false objects of attainment (*mithyāsādhya*) and false principles (*mithyātattva*) are [described in] the *Pañcapradīpa*, *Amṛtabindu*, and *Candra*...
The mandalas arise from the bindu between the eyebrows.
The nature of wind, beginning with the uvula in the throat and so forth, is not of the nature of the principles (tattva); this must be inferred by oneself. || 18 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *pañcapradīpa* and so forth: some maintain that the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is the constant practice of that which is characterized by the "five lamps" (*pañcapradīpa*), namely the *gokudaha* [the five products of the cow], and that which is characterized by the "nectar" (*amṛta*), namely the *vimumāraśula*. Others, considering the "drop" (*bindu*) to be the intensely radiant reality situated within the moon of the heart, meditate upon it as the goal. Still others meditate on the "moon" (*candra*)—either in the form of a digit (*kalā*) or as a half-moon—situated within the heart-lotus.

"Maṇḍalas arising from the drop at the center of the eyebrows" means that one should visualize a drop (*bindu*) between the two eyebrows at the *ūrṇā* [hair-tuft]; from that drop arise the maṇḍalas characterized as those of Vāyu, Varuṇa, Mahendra, and Agni. This is what is meant: having covered the mouth, ears, eyes, nose, and tongue with the fingers of the hands, the drop at the center of the eyebrows is to be observed. When that [drop] reaches a state of clarity, the maṇḍalas of Mahendra and the others arise, indicating auspicious and inauspicious signs.
And they consider that drop to be the *tattva*.

The nature of *vāyu* consists of the characteristics of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and the state of total tranquility, as well as the characteristics of the incoming and outgoing breaths (*ānāpāna*). This is what is meant: having understood the nature of *vāyu* as taught in the Śaiva, Sāṃkhya, and other systems, and having stabilized that *vāyu* through the meditation on its restraint, the proponents of *vāyu* directly realize everything from leaping into the sky and entering the bodies of others up to liberation itself.

Regarding "the throat-pendant" (*galaśuṇḍikā*): in the region of the throat, above the root of the tongue, there is a fleshy growth shaped like an elephant’s trunk that hangs downward; it is known as the *upajihvā* (sub-tongue) and is called the throat-pendant. It is of the nature of power (*śakti*). Beneath it exists the reality (*tattva*) in the form of Śiva. When touched by the tip of the tongue, it flows with an uninterrupted stream of nectar. One should meditate upon oneself being satiated by that downpour of gurgling nectar; this is the reality of the throat-pendant.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such [statements] as: "One should meditate upon the reality (*tattva*) whose nature is consciousness and whose form is Śiva, situated in the center of the wheel of sixteen channels (*nāḍī*) in the middle of the heart.

All of that which is accepted by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others as being the nature of reality is, in fact, not reality; this is what must be inferred and investigated by oneself—this is the conclusion.
By means of dreams, magical illusions, reflections, illusions, mirages, cities of the Gandharvas, the moon in water,
and other such terms denoting similes;
There is nothing to be accomplished here other than what has been described. || 19 ||

"Like a dream, like a magical illusion," and so forth. By means of such words as "resembling a dream, a magical illusion, a reflection, an illusion, a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, or the moon in water," and by other words expressing similes—such as "resembling an echo in the sky, foam," and so on—which denote comparisons, there is indeed nothing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) other than what has already been stated as the goal. However, one should understand for oneself that these words function here precisely with respect to the goal already mentioned.
[This is expressed] through words such as "profound," "empty," "mere appearance," "quiescent," "extremely subtle," and "inexpressible."
One should not entertain the delusion that there exists another reality to be accomplished through means such as being "unstained," "formless," or "untainted."

It is profound emptiness, mere appearance, peaceful, extremely subtle, inexpressible, untainted, formless, stainless, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [terms such as] auspicious (*śiva*), formless (*nirākāra*), free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), and without beginning, end, or destruction are included. One should not entertain the delusion that there exists some other goal (*sādhya*) beyond these. Nor should one entertain the delusion that there is some other goal superior to what has been described. Rather, the certainty is that the goal itself is not described at all by any of these terms.
Whatever merit I have acquired from this work consisting of words composed in seven ways, which pervades the entire interior of space, through its dedication—
By him, who has manifested a body endowed with the knowledge of incomparable bliss and who has accomplished the welfare of beings, may this world be benefited. 21.
The *Tattvaratnāvaloka* is completed. This work is by the venerable Paṇḍita Vāgīśvarakīrti.
This composition of that Vāgīśvara, whose supreme devotion and stainless steadfastness toward the *Śrīsamāja* are well-known, destroys all doubt.
And whatever merit has been accumulated by me, which resembles blooming white water-lilies, stars, and jasmine, and is bound together from this [work],
may it result in one who is filled with incomparable bliss and embraced by innate gnosis (*svābhavidyā*).
May he, through that [merit], become the glory of the Lord of Speech for all the world.
The *Tattvaratnāvalokavivaraṇa* is completed. This work is the composition of the venerable scholar-teacher Vāgīśvarakīrti.
